claim: The midbrain raphe nuclei contain the majority of forebrain-projecting serotonergic neurons in mammals.
source: The midbrain raphe nuclei contain the majority of forebrain-projecting serotonergic neurons in mammals (Jacobs and Azmitia, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacobs and Azmitia, 1992

claim: The mouse dorsal raphe contains approximately 9000 serotonergic neurons.
source: This small population of neurons (approximately 9000 in the mouse dorsal raphe; Ishimura et al., 1988)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ishimura et al., 1988

claim: Serotonergic neurons project to almost the entire forebrain.
source: This small population of neurons (approximately 9000 in the mouse dorsal raphe; Ishimura et al., 1988) projects to almost the entire forebrain (Azmitia and Segal, 1978; Moore et al., 1978; Steinbusch, 1981; O'Hearn and Molliver, 1984; Vertes, 1991; Gagnon and Parent, 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: About two-thirds of dorsal raphe neurons are serotonergic.
source: About two-thirds of dorsal raphe neurons are serotonergic, but others contain GABA, glutamate, dopamine, acetylcholine, or various peptides (Hökfelt et al., 2000; Commons, 2009; Fu et al., 2010; Hioki et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: ChR2 expression in serotonergic neurons was specific, with 2.3% of ChR2-EYFP-positive cells being 5-HT-negative.
source: Expression was specific (of 260 ChR2-EYFP-positive cells, 6 cells, or 2.3%, were 5-HT-negative)
evidence: Supported by cell counting data from immunohistochemistry

claim: ChR2 expression in serotonergic neurons was efficient, with 80.9% of 5-HT-positive cells being ChR2-EYFP-positive.
source: Expression was specific (of 260 ChR2-EYFP-positive cells, 6 cells, or 2.3%, were 5-HT-negative) and efficient (of 314 5-HT-positive cells, 254, or 80.9%, were ChR2-EYFP-positive; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 1D

claim: 29 neurons were identified as serotonergic neurons based on their responses to light stimulation.
source: 29 neurons fell into the former cluster (filled cyan points in Figure 2B). Three points in that cluster were not considered identified serotonergic neurons because they did not reliably respond to light stimulation.
evidence: Based on clustering analysis of light-evoked responses shown in Figure 2B

claim: All 29 identified serotonergic neurons showed fast light-evoked spikes.
source: Consistent with direct light activation rather than indirect synaptic activation, all 29 neurons showed fast light-evoked spikes (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: All 29 identified serotonergic neurons followed high-frequency stimulation.
source: Consistent with direct light activation rather than indirect synaptic activation, all 29 neurons showed fast light-evoked spikes (Figure 2C) and followed high-frequency stimulation (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 2D and 2E

claim: All 29 serotonergic neurons exhibited task-related modulations in firing rate.
source: All 29 serotonergic neurons exhibited task-related modulations in firing rate (ANOVA, all p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of firing rates

claim: 41% of serotonergic neurons fired at a higher or lower rate during the ITIs of reward blocks vs punishment blocks.
source: First, a large fraction (41%) of serotonergic neurons fired at a higher or lower rate during the ITIs of reward blocks vs punishment blocks (Figure 3A,B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A, B and supplement

claim: 12 of 29 serotonergic neurons showed significantly different pre-trial firing rates between reward and punishment blocks.
source: 12 of 29 serotonergic neurons showed significantly different pre-trial firing rates between reward and punishment blocks: 7 were more excited during reward blocks, 5 were more excited during punishment blocks (Figure 3C,D; Wilcoxon rank sum tests, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 3C and 3D

claim: 7 serotonergic neurons were more excited during reward blocks than punishment blocks.
source: 12 of 29 serotonergic neurons showed significantly different pre-trial firing rates between reward and punishment blocks: 7 were more excited during reward blocks, 5 were more excited during punishment blocks (Figure 3C,D; Wilcoxon rank sum tests, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 3C and 3D

claim: 5 serotonergic neurons were more excited during punishment blocks than reward blocks.
source: 12 of 29 serotonergic neurons showed significantly different pre-trial firing rates between reward and punishment blocks: 7 were more excited during reward blocks, 5 were more excited during punishment blocks (Figure 3C,D; Wilcoxon rank sum tests, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 3C and 3D

claim: 16 of 29 serotonergic neurons displayed gradually decreasing firing rates over the course of the experiment.
source: In addition, 16 of 29 serotonergic neurons displayed gradually decreasing firing rates over the course of the experiment (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: None of the dopaminergic neurons showed significantly different pre-trial firing rates between reward and punishment blocks.
source: None of the putative or identified dopaminergic neurons showed significantly different pre-trial firing rates between reward and punishment blocks (Wilcoxon rank sum tests, all p > 0.5; Figure 3E–H).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 3E-H

claim: 28 out of 29 serotonergic neurons responded phasically to punishments.
source: Most serotonergic neurons (28 out of 29) responded phasically to punishments: 22 were excited, 6 were inhibited (Figure 4A–C; Wilcoxon rank sum tests in the 500 ms after punishment onset, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 4A-C

claim: 22 serotonergic neurons were excited by punishments.
source: Most serotonergic neurons (28 out of 29) responded phasically to punishments: 22 were excited, 6 were inhibited (Figure 4A–C; Wilcoxon rank sum tests in the 500 ms after punishment onset, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 4A-C

claim: 6 serotonergic neurons were inhibited by punishments.
source: Most serotonergic neurons (28 out of 29) responded phasically to punishments: 22 were excited, 6 were inhibited (Figure 4A–C; Wilcoxon rank sum tests in the 500 ms after punishment onset, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 4A-C

claim: The response of serotonergic neurons to punishments was transient, lasting less than 500 ms for most neurons (315 ± 140 ms, mean ± S.D.).
source: This response was transient, lasting less than 500 ms for most neurons (315 ± 140 ms, mean ± S.D.).
evidence: Supported by analysis of response duration

claim: About half of serotonergic neurons (15 out of 29) were phasically excited by reward-predicting cues.
source: About half of serotonergic neurons (15 out of 29) were phasically excited by reward-predicting cues (Figure 4D–F; Wilcoxon rank sum tests during the 1 s of odor presentation, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 4D-F

claim: Very few serotonergic neurons (2 out of 29) were inhibited by reward-predicting cues.
source: Very few neurons (2 out of 29; p < 0.05) were inhibited by reward-predicting cues.
evidence: Supported by statistical tests

claim: The duration of excitation by reward-predicting cues was brief, lasting less than 500 ms (235 ± 194 ms, mean ± S.D.).
source: The duration of excitation was brief, lasting less than 500 ms (235 ± 194 ms, mean ± S.D.).
evidence: Supported by analysis of response duration

claim: For 9 of 15 serotonergic neurons excited by reward-predicting cues, the response to a reward-predicting CS was significantly greater than the response to a punishment-predicting CS.
source: For 9 of these 15 neurons, the response to a reward-predicting CS was significantly greater than the response to a punishment-predicting CS (Wilcoxon rank sum tests, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests

claim: The time of peak response during a reward-predicting CS was significantly shorter for serotonergic than dopaminergic neurons.
source: The time of peak response during a reward-predicting CS was significantly shorter for serotonergic than dopaminergic neurons (mean ± S.E.M., 331 ± 15.7 ms for serotonergic neurons, 388 ± 12.7 ms for dopaminergic neurons, Wilcoxon rank sum test, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of response timing

claim: 11 of 29 serotonergic neurons were significantly excited by unexpected rewards.
source: Whereas dopaminergic neurons showed a large, phasic excitation in response to unexpected rewards, a subset of serotonergic neurons was weakly and slowly, but significantly, excited (Wilcoxon rank sum tests, p < 0.05 for 9 of 10 dopaminergic neurons and 11 of 29 serotonergic neurons; Figure 4G,H).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 4G and 4H

claim: Serotonergic neurons showed a weak but significantly larger response to unexpected vs expected rewards.
source: Interestingly, serotonergic neurons showed a weak but significantly larger response to unexpected vs expected rewards (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4I

claim: The difference in pre-trial firing rate during reward vs punishment blocks positively correlated with the difference in response to reward- vs punishment-predicting CS.
source: We found that the difference in pre-trial firing rate during reward vs punishment blocks positively correlated with the difference in response to reward- vs punishment-predicting CS; neurons with higher excitation for reward than punishment CS tended to fire at a higher rate before reward than punishment trials (Figure 5A; Pearson's r = 0.85, t27 = 8.56, p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The difference in pre-trial firing rate (reward vs punishment) did not significantly correlate with the response to punishment.
source: The difference in pre-trial firing rate (reward vs punishment) did not significantly correlate with the response to punishment (Figure 5B; Pearson's r = 0.03, t27 = −0.17, p > 0.8).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The response to reward CS was significantly positively correlated with the response to punishment.
source: The response to reward CS was significantly positively correlated with the response to punishment (Figure 5C; Pearson's r = 0.60, t27 = 3.89, p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and data shown in Figure 5C

claim: For 7 of 8 serotonergic neurons with significantly different pre-trial firing rates during reward vs punishment blocks, pre-trial firing rates during neutral blocks did not fall outside of the bounds of those during reward and punishment blocks.
source: For 7 of these 8 neurons (3 of which displayed higher firing rates during reward blocks, 5 of which displayed higher firing rates during punishment blocks), pre-trial firing rates during neutral blocks did not fall outside of the bounds of those during reward and punishment blocks (Figure 6A; Tukey's Honest Significant Difference tests, p > 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Only 1 of 16 serotonergic neurons had significantly larger pre-trial firing rates during neutral blocks than during reward and punishment blocks.
source: Only 1 of the 16 neurons had both significantly larger pre-trial firing rates during neutral blocks than during reward and punishment blocks.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: 15 of 16 serotonergic neurons were not salience-coding across blocks of trials.
source: Thus, 15 of 16 serotonergic neurons were not salience-coding across blocks of trials.
evidence: Based on analysis of firing rates during neutral vs reward and punishment blocks

claim: For 13 serotonergic neurons tested with three reward sizes, firing rates were either strictly increasing (5 neurons) or strictly decreasing (8 neurons) with reward size.
source: Indeed, for each of the 13 neurons, firing rates were either strictly increasing (5 neurons) or strictly decreasing (8 neurons) with reward size (Figure 6B; Tukey's Honest Significant Difference tests, p > 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figure 6B

claim: 8 of 21 serotonergic neurons were tonically more (6 neurons) or less (2 neurons) active in water vs quinine blocks, during ITIs.
source: We found that 8 of these 21 neurons were tonically more (6 neurons) or less (2 neurons) active in water vs quinine blocks, during ITIs (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 6C and 6D

claim: 20 of 50 identified serotonergic neurons showed tonic differences in firing for reward vs punishment blocks of trials.
source: Across both experiments, 20 of 50 identified serotonergic neurons showed tonic differences in firing for reward vs punishment blocks of trials.
evidence: Summary of data from multiple experiments

claim: For serotonergic neurons, the CS-induced firing rate as a function of value was monotonic.
source: For each of the 23 serotonergic neurons with sufficient data for this analysis, the CS-induced firing rate as a function of value was monotonic (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 7A and 7B

claim: As a population, the CS firing rate of serotonergic neurons was larger for reward than punishment.
source: As a population, the CS firing rate was larger for reward than punishment (paired t-test, t22 = 2.6, p < 0.05)
evidence: Supported by statistical test

claim: As a population, the CS firing rate of serotonergic neurons was larger for reward than neutral.
source: As a population, the CS firing rate was larger for reward than punishment (paired t-test, t22 = 2.6, p < 0.05), larger for reward than neutral (t22 = 2.9, p < 0.05)
evidence: Supported by statistical test

claim: As a population, the CS firing rate of serotonergic neurons was larger for neutral than punishment.
source: As a population, the CS firing rate was larger for reward than punishment (paired t-test, t22 = 2.6, p < 0.05), larger for reward than neutral (t22 = 2.9, p < 0.05), and larger for neutral than punishment (t22 = 2.2, p < 0.05; Figure 7C–E).
evidence: Supported by statistical test and data shown in Figures 7C-E

claim: 29 of 120 unidentified neurons showed significantly different pre-trial firing rates between reward and punishment blocks.
source: 29 of 120 unidentified neurons showed significantly different pre-trial firing rates between reward and punishment blocks: 10 were more excited during reward blocks, 19 were more excited during punishment blocks (Figure 8C,D, Wilcoxon rank sum tests, p < 0.05).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figures 8C and 8D

claim: 92 of 120 unidentified neurons showed task-related responses during the trial.
source: In addition to these slow firing-rate fluctuations across minutes, 92 of 120 unidentified neurons showed task-related responses during the trial (ANOVA, all p < 0.01; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA and data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claim: Serotonergic neuron responses during the trial epoch tended to be more phasic than those of the 92 task-responsive unidentified neurons.
source: That is, serotonergic neuron responses during the trial epoch (from CS to US) tended to be more phasic than those of the 92 task-responsive unidentified neurons (Fisher's exact test on the proportion of 100-ms bins significantly different from baseline, odds ratio = 0.643, p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical test

claim: Serotonergic neurons had significantly longer spike duration than unidentified neurons.
source: Serotonergic neurons had significantly longer spike duration than unidentified neurons (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p < 0.05), although there was significant overlap in the distributions (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical test and data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A

claim: There was no significant difference between the mean firing rate of serotonergic and unidentified neurons.
source: There was no significant difference between the mean firing rate (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p > 0.6)
evidence: Supported by statistical test and data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A

claim: There was no significant difference in the coefficient of variation of the inter-spike interval distributions between serotonergic and unidentified neurons.
source: There was no significant difference between the mean firing rate (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A; Wilcoxon rank sum test, p > 0.6) or coefficient of variation of the inter-spike interval distributions (Wilcoxon rank sum test, p > 0.1) between serotonergic and unidentified neurons.
evidence: Supported by statistical test

claim: Neither an expectation-maximization nor a k-means clustering algorithm could classify serotonergic neurons based on spike duration, firing rate, or shape of the inter-spike interval distribution.
source: Neither an expectation-maximization nor a k-means clustering algorithm could classify serotonergic neurons based on spike duration, firing rate, or shape of the inter-spike interval distribution.
evidence: Based on clustering analysis

claim: Mice licked significantly more during reward trials than neutral or punishment trials.
source: Mice licked toward the water-delivery tube in the delay period before rewards arrived, but not during neutral or punishment trials, indicating that they had learned the CS-US associations (analysis of variance (ANOVA), t-tests, p < 0.001 for each session; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests and data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Mice licked significantly more during the tone preceding reward vs punishment blocks.
source: Mice licked significantly more during the tone preceding reward vs punishment blocks. Because the tone was the same preceding both block types, this indicates that they attended to the block structure (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.01; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical test and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Mice reliably chose water reward without air puff over water reward with air puff, confirming that air puffs act as a negative reinforcement.
source: Mice reliably chose the water reward without the air puff, confirming that air puffs act as a negative reinforcement (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral choice data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The tonic signal in serotonergic neurons appeared to build up or down slowly within blocks, rather than sharply increasing or decreasing in response to block transitions.
source: Interestingly, this tonic signal appeared to build up or down slowly within blocks, rather than sharply increasing or decreasing in response to block transitions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The tonic signal in serotonergic neurons did not depend on the duration of ITIs.
source: This tonic signal did not depend on the duration of ITIs (Wilcoxon rank sum tests, all p > 0.3).
evidence: Supported by statistical tests

claim: Serotonergic neurons signal information about reward and punishment on multiple timescales.
source: These results suggest that serotonergic neurons signal information about reward and punishment on multiple timescales.
evidence: Based on the three main features of serotonergic neuron activity observed in the study

claim: A large fraction of serotonergic neurons modulated their tonic firing rates over the course of minutes during reward vs punishment blocks.
source: We found three main features of serotonergic neuron activity: (1) a large fraction of serotonergic neurons modulated their tonic firing rates over the course of minutes during reward vs punishment blocks
evidence: Summary of main finding from the study

claim: Most serotonergic neurons were phasically excited by punishments.
source: We found three main features of serotonergic neuron activity: (1) a large fraction of serotonergic neurons modulated their tonic firing rates over the course of minutes during reward vs punishment blocks; (2) most were phasically excited by punishments
evidence: Summary of main finding from the study

claim: A subset of serotonergic neurons was phasically excited by reward-predicting cues.
source: We found three main features of serotonergic neuron activity: (1) a large fraction of serotonergic neurons modulated their tonic firing rates over the course of minutes during reward vs punishment blocks; (2) most were phasically excited by punishments; and (3) a subset was phasically excited by reward-predicting cues.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the study

claim: Dopaminergic neurons did not show firing rate changes across blocks of trials.
source: By contrast, dopaminergic neurons did not show firing rate changes across blocks of trials.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the study

claim: The same serotonergic neurons can multiplex different signals about reward and punishment on different timescales.
source: This demonstrates that the same serotonergic neurons can multiplex different signals about reward and punishment on different timescales.
evidence: Based on the correlation between pre-trial firing rate differences and CS response differences

claim: Background firing rate in serotonergic neurons signal value across different magnitudes of reward and different types of punishment.
source: Thus, background firing rate in serotonergic neurons signal value across different magnitudes of reward and different types of punishment.
evidence: Based on experiments with different reward sizes and different punishment types

claim: Firing rate differences between reward and punishment trials reflected the value, not the salience, of those stimuli.
source: This suggests that firing rate differences between reward and punishment trials reflected the value, not the salience, of those stimuli.
evidence: Based on analysis of CS firing rates for reward, neutral, and punishment trials

claim: 149 dorsal raphe neurons were recorded while mice performed the conditioning task.
source: We recorded the activity of 149 dorsal raphe neurons while mice performed the conditioning task (6 mice, 24.8 ± 6.1 neurons per mouse, mean ± S.E.M.).
evidence: Description of experimental data collection

claim: 28 ventral tegmental area neurons were recorded, 15 of which were identified as dopaminergic.
source: To compare this effect to the response of dopaminergic neurons—which have been proposed to be involved in long-term value-related signaling (Niv et al., 2006; Cools et al., 2011)—in the same task, we recorded the activity of 28 ventral tegmental area (VTA) neurons, 15 of which were identified as dopaminergic (by ChR2 tagging, as described above), and 13 of which were putatively dopaminergic based on their task-related responses (4 mice, 7.0 ± 2.0 neurons per mouse, mean ± S.E.M.).
evidence: Description of experimental data collection

claim: 50 serotonergic neurons were identified across all experiments.
source: Identified serotonergic neurons, of which there were 50 across experiments, came from all nine mice (a range of 1–10 per mouse).
evidence: Summary of total identified neurons across experiments

claim: All neurons in the data set had L-ratios < 0.05 and signal-to-noise ratios of > 5 dB.
source: All neurons in the data set had L-ratios < 0.05 and signal-to-noise ratios of > 5 dB.
evidence: Description of data quality criteria
